blogs.title: A Statutory "Shall" Without a Plaintiff: What America First Legal Says About Procedural Rights and Article III
blogs.description: This post would examine the opinion’s core move: treating OSC’s alleged duty to investigate under 5 U.S.C. § 1216 as a bare procedural entitlement that cannot support standing without a separate concrete interest. It would situate the decision alongside Summers, Alliance for Hippocratic Medicine, and recent D.C. Circuit standing cases, and ask whether the court is increasingly using injury, causation, and redressability to keep private plaintiffs from enforcing statutory commands directed at agency oversight bodies.

blogs.title: The Question the D.C. Circuit Left Open: How Section 1216 Interacts With FOIA’s Own OSC Referral Mechanism
blogs.description: This post would focus on the merits question the panel never reached: whether § 1216 gives OSC freestanding authority—or even a duty—to investigate arbitrary FOIA withholdings outside the more specific trigger in 5 U.S.C. § 552(a)(4)(F). It would explain why the district court’s now-vacated reading matters, what uncertainty remains for agencies and requesters, and how the case leaves FOIA’s disciplinary architecture notably unsettled.

blogs.title: Informational Standing Has Limits: Why a Hope for Investigative "Fruits" Is Not a Right to Information
blogs.description: This post would unpack the court’s rejection of AFL’s second theory of standing and the opinion’s careful distinction between a statutory entitlement to receive information and a contingent hope that an agency investigation might generate useful notices or disclosures. It would compare the case to Akins and Public Citizen, and explore how the decision narrows efforts to repackage agency-process claims as informational injuries.

blogs.title: Redressability Through a Chain of Agency Discretion: OSC, MSPB, DOJ, and the Post-Chaney Standing Problem
blogs.description: This post would analyze the opinion’s most practical lesson for administrative litigants: when requested relief depends on a cascade of discretionary decisions by multiple agencies, standing will be hard to establish. Using the court’s OSC-to-MSPB-to-DOJ chain, it would explore how Heckler v. Chaney, Brackeen, and Hecate Energy are reshaping redressability analysis in suits that seek to force one agency to police another.
